4 · One fact, five ways of reporting it.
The units are empty.  →  the present situation.
The units were originally shops.  →  how it began.

Objections are usually raised about parking.  →  what happens as a rule.

1 · Read the explanation.
Three time frames in one short report

A report describes a situation, gives its background and records what was said about it. Each of those needs a different form, and the commonest fault in a weak report is that all three are written in the past simple.

The situation now takes the present simple: several units are empty, the street belongs to the council. Add currently or at present if you want to signal that it may change. What happens as a rule also takes the present simple, with a frequency adverb in mid position: objections are always raised at this stage, the committee usually meets in March.

The background takes used to and would for past practices, and originally for how something began: the units were originally shops, the council used to hold these meetings twice a year. What happened at the meeting takes the past simple: two councillors objected, the chair wrapped up the discussion at nine.

Adverbs do the rest. Adverbs of manner say how something was done and usually sit before the verb in this kind of writing: firmly believe, strongly oppose, fully accept. Degree adverbs say how much and stand in front of the adjective: considerably cheaper, slightly higher, far more likely. And English softens criticism with a small set of phrases rather than with weaker words: not exactly, not entirely, somewhat, arguably.

Register in a report
  • Impersonal where possible: it was agreed that… rather than we said we would…
  • No contractions: did not, will not.
  • Attribute opinions: one councillor argued that…, not the plan is stupid.
  • Numbers where you have them: two of the eleven units beats several units.
2 · Study the examples.
PatternExample

Two things to watch

1 — Do not report a present situation in the past. The units were empty tells the reader they may no longer be. If they still are, write are currently empty. This single choice decides whether a report is useful next month.

2 — Adverb, not adjective, with the verb. The proposal was firm supported and rents are considerable lower are the two most frequent slips at this level; the second is the one that survives into otherwise good writing.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Then, now, and how often

A report needs three time layers and keeps them apart. The present simple states the situation as it stands: Nine of the eleven units are currently empty · The committee meets on the first Tuesday of the month. used to and would give the practice before: The council used to hold these meetings twice a year · Each spring the owners would repaint the fronts. The past simple reports the meeting itself: Two councillors objected; one abstained.

originally, currently and now let you put then and now in a single sentence: The units were originally shops; they are currently empty. Frequency adverbs sit in mid position — before the main verb, after be: Objections are always raised at this stage.

Saying how, how much, and how bluntly

Adverbs of manner say how something was done and normally follow the verb or its object: The chair firmly rejected the second proposal · The plan was strongly opposed. Degree adverbs go in front of the adjective or comparative they modify: considerably lower · slightly higher · far more likely. Note that far, much and considerably can strengthen a comparative but not a plain adjective: far cheap → far cheaper.

The register of a written report is careful rather than blunt, and English does that with fixed softeners: not entirely clear, not altogether convincing, it wouldn’t exactly help, there is some doubt about. And a claim that is not yours gets attributed: One councillor argued that…, According to the surveyor… Reporting rather than asserting is what makes a report sound professional.

Errors to watch: Objections always are raised → are always raised · rents are considerably low → considerably lower · the units are originally shops → were originally shops · it is not exactly clear entirely — use one softener, not three.

  • Interrupt early, with a question rather than an objection.
  • Raise the cost, and what else the money would buy.
  • Say what would make you support it.
  • Interrupt once more, at the worst possible moment.

Work in pairs. Five minutes. Then swap roles, so that each of you chairs and objects.Five minutes with your teacher, then swap roles and do the other part.

Afterwards: one interruption that improved the meeting, and one that only delayed it.

6 · Write the report of that meeting. 180–220 words.
Include
  • a first paragraph on the space: originally, and currently;
  • what usually happens there, with a frequency adverb;
  • the proposal and its cost, in the past simple as it was put to the meeting;
  • the objection, attributed to whoever made it and softened;
  • at least four items from stage 2 and two degree adverbs;
  • a closing recommendation beginning To summarize.

4 · Read the model report.
Model · a short report to a council committee

The site. The square behind the bus station was originally a market and has been a car park since 1996. Eleven of its forty spaces are currently unused on an average weekday, and the surface has not been repaired for nine years. The space is crossed by most of the people who walk between the station and the college, and complaints are always about the same two things: the state of the ground and the absence of any light after four in the afternoon.

The proposal. At the meeting of 14 March it was proposed that half the car park be closed and turned into a lit public square, at a cost of approximately eleven million tenge. The chair pointed out that the college had offered to pay a third of that, and that the work would take a single summer.

The objections. Two members argued that the loss of parking would not exactly help local businesses, which are already considerably weaker than they were before the new centre opened. One of them added that a lit square is more likely to attract noise than customers. Both accepted that the surface has to be repaired in any case.

To summarize, the disagreement is not about the square but about the parking. I recommend closing a third of the spaces rather than half, and reviewing the decision after one winter.
